items.prompt: Which document lists a role's main duties, required skills and reporting line?

options.label: Reference check form
Onboarding plan
Job description
Offer letter

rubric: A job description sets out the duties, requirements and reporting line for a role.
An offer letter comes at the end and states pay and terms, which is a common mix-up.

items.prompt: In a structured interview, which feature is always present?

options.label: Each candidate gets the same planned questions
Candidates choose which topics are discussed
Only the manager's first impression is recorded
Questions change based on the interviewer's mood

rubric: Structured interviews use the same predetermined questions for every candidate.
Other options describe unstructured interviews, which allow inconsistency.

items.prompt: What is the name for a scoring guide that describes what weak, adequate and strong answers look like?

options.label: Exit survey
Anchored rating scale
Talent pipeline
Salary band

rubric: An anchored rating scale defines each score level with example answers.
A salary band is about pay, not scoring answers.

items.prompt: In the STAR method for answering interview questions, what does the letter R stand for?

options.label: Reflection
Requirement
Responsibility
Result

rubric: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Reflection and Responsibility sound plausible but are not part of the acronym.

items.prompt: Which step should come first in a hiring process?

options.label: Holding the final interview
Defining the role's needs
Making the offer
Checking references

rubric: The role must be defined before sourcing and assessing anyone.
Later steps cannot be judged fairly without agreed requirements.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common ways to source candidates? Select all that apply.

options.label: University career events
Employee referrals
Payroll records of current staff
Online job boards
Annual reviews of current staff

rubric: Referrals, job boards and career events are standard sourcing channels.
Payroll records and reviews are internal records, not sourcing channels.

items.prompt: A recruiter receives 120 applications for an analyst role. She compares each résumé with the must-have requirements in the job description to decide who gets a phone call. Which hiring stage is she performing?

options.label: Offer negotiation
Sourcing
Screening
Onboarding

rubric: Screening narrows applicants against defined requirements.
Sourcing is attracting applicants, which has already happened here.

items.prompt: Why do structured interviews usually lead to fairer decisions than unstructured ones?

options.label: Interviewers can skip questions they find awkward or irrelevant to a candidate
Interviewers can rely on their first impression more confidently and quickly
Every candidate faces the same questions, so answers can be compared
Candidates feel more relaxed with a set script, so they talk for longer

rubric: Identical questions and scoring allow like-for-like comparison.
Instinct and skipped questions add inconsistency and bias.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to separate must-have from nice-to-have criteria before screening begins?

options.label: It lets the team adjust the criteria once they have seen the first strong applicants
It lets the advert stay short, since nice-to-haves can then be left out of it
It keeps screening consistent and stops extras from outweighing essentials
It lets the team rank candidates on overall impression rather than on set criteria

rubric: Agreed priorities keep screening consistent and evidence-based.
Changing criteria after seeing candidates invites bias.

items.prompt: A candidate prepares two or three STAR stories before an interview. Why does this help?

options.label: It means they no longer need to research the role or the employer
It gives concrete evidence of past behaviour in an organised way
It lets them steer every question toward the same rehearsed story
It shows the interviewer they have a polished, memorised script

rubric: STAR stories give specific, structured evidence of what the candidate did.
Preparation does not replace understanding the role or answering the question.

items.prompt: An interviewer asks: "What would you do if a teammate missed a deadline that affected your work?" How is this question best classified?

options.label: Brain teaser testing logic puzzles
Illegal question about personal life
Situational question about a possible case
Behavioural question about a real past event

rubric: It poses a hypothetical, so it is situational.
Behavioural questions ask about real past experiences, such as "Tell me about a time...".

items.prompt: Three interviewers each ask different questions and rate candidates on gut feeling. What is the most likely result?

options.label: Ratings are consistent because experienced people agree
Ratings are hard to compare and prone to bias
Ratings match job performance more closely
Ratings become more objective through variety

rubric: Different questions and gut ratings make comparison unreliable and open to bias.
Variety without shared criteria does not create objectivity.

items.prompt: Which practices help make an interview process fairer? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rejecting candidates who seem not to be a culture fit by feel
Rating candidates independently before group discussion
Asking about candidates' family plans to assess availability
Scoring each answer against a rubric during the interview
Asking every candidate the same core questions

rubric: Rubrics, same questions and independent ratings reduce bias.
Gut-feel culture fit and family questions introduce bias or are inappropriate.

items.prompt: During an interview, a hiring manager discovers the candidate attended her old university. She spends most of the time reminiscing and skips her planned questions, then rates the candidate highly. What is the main problem with this approach?

options.label: Reminiscing is unprofessional and may make the candidate uncomfortable
Shared university history should count as a main hiring criterion
Affinity bias replaced job evidence, so the rating is unsupported
Shared background is irrelevant, so the interview should have been shorter

rubric: Liking someone for a shared trait is affinity bias; skipping questions leaves no job-related evidence.
Rapport is fine, but it should not replace the structured questions.

items.prompt: Why do structured interviews usually predict job performance better than unstructured ones?

options.label: Interviewers can follow rapport freely, which lets candidates relax and reveals their true personality and fit
Panels are larger, so more opinions are averaged and any single interviewer's judgement matters much less
Every candidate gets the same questions and is scored on the same criteria, so evidence is comparable
Questions are kept secret from candidates, so nobody can prepare and the answers are more honest in the end

rubric: Standard questions and shared scoring criteria make candidates comparable on job-related evidence.
Distractors confuse structure with rapport, secrecy or panel size.

items.prompt: Which of these is a behavioural interview question?

options.label: How would you handle a deadline that suddenly moved forward next quarter?
Do you consider yourself good at working under deadline pressure?
What do you think makes a team successful when deadlines are tight?
Tell me about a time you had to deliver a project after a key deadline moved.

rubric: Behavioural questions ask about real past behaviour.
The hypothetical, self-rating and opinion questions elicit predictions or views, not past evidence.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to define a role's scorecard of required skills before sourcing candidates?

options.label: It lets the team keep criteria flexible, adding requirements as strong candidates appear during screening
It lets recruiters advertise the role at a higher salary band because the duties list looks longer and more detailed
It fixes the criteria before candidates are seen, so people are judged on role needs rather than on who applies
It replaces interviews, since a well-written description already shows which applicants will perform best

rubric: Setting criteria in advance keeps judgement tied to the role, not to the candidates who happen to apply.
Flexible criteria let preferences drift toward the people already seen.

items.prompt: Why should each interviewer write notes and submit scores before the panel discusses a candidate?

options.label: Scoring first stops early or senior opinions from anchoring others, so the panel gets independent evidence
It lets the most experienced interviewer overrule weaker scores by recording their rating at the very end
It guarantees all interviewers give the same score, because notes remove differences in interpretation
It saves time because the discussion can be skipped when the written scores are close enough together

rubric: Independent scoring protects against anchoring and conformity in group discussion.
Distractors assume scoring replaces discussion or guarantees agreement.

items.prompt: As a candidate, why is it helpful to prepare examples using the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result)?

options.label: It keeps answers very short, because interviewers score brevity above the amount of detail in examples
It shifts focus to team achievements, because interviewers discount what individual candidates claim to have done
It lets you give the same polished answer to any question, so you need not tailor examples to the role
It grounds answers in a real situation, your actions and the result, giving the interviewer concrete evidence

rubric: STAR gives specific, evidence-rich answers to behavioural questions.
Distractors misread it as a generic script, a brevity rule or a way to hide individual contribution.

items.prompt: Which of the following are features of a structured interview? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each candidate is asked the same core questions
The final score is one overall gut-feel rating given at the end
Each answer is rated against job-related criteria as it is given
Scoring anchors describe what weak and strong answers look like
Interviewers pick questions freely depending on how well they click with the candidate

rubric: Consistent questions, scoring anchors and per-answer rating define structure.
Free choice of questions and one gut-feel score remove the consistency structure provides.

items.prompt: A hiring manager says, 'I don't need a scorecard; I'll know the right person when I meet them.' Six candidates are booked for interviews, and the manager plans to ask each one different questions based on their CV. What is the main risk of this approach?

options.label: The interviews will produce too much evidence, making the final decision slower than a scorecard process would
The company will break employment law automatically, because any process without a scorecard is unlawful
Criteria form after meeting people, so rapport and similarity can outweigh job-related evidence
Candidates will find the interviews too long, and strong applicants may withdraw before the final round

rubric: Without preset criteria and common questions, decisions follow gut feeling and similarity, not comparable evidence.
Distractors name length, evidence overload or automatic illegality, which are not the core issue.

items.prompt: A scorecard weights technical skill 50%, communication 30% and collaboration 20%. A candidate scores 4, 3 and 5 out of 5 respectively. What is the weighted score?
rubric: 4.0 is the unweighted average; 4.2 applies the weights in reverse order.

items.prompt: In an interview a candidate says, 'We cut onboarding time by improving the process.' Which follow-up question best draws out useful evidence?

options.label: How large was the company, and did the team around you generally get along well?
That sounds impressive, so can you tell me which other achievements you are proud of?
Would you use the same approach if you were hired here, and why would it work?
What exactly did you do yourself, and how did you measure the change in onboarding time?

rubric: Probing for personal actions and measured results tests the claim with specific evidence.
The other questions accept the claim or move to unrelated topics.

items.prompt: A role requires travel two weeks a month. Which question should the interviewer ask to check this fairly?

options.label: This role involves travel two weeks a month; are you able to meet that requirement?
Most people with young children avoid travel, so would this role suit your current situation?
Are you planning to start a family soon, since this role involves frequent travel each month?
Do you have family commitments that would make frequent travel difficult for you to manage?

rubric: Fair questions ask about the job requirement, asked of everyone, not about family circumstances.
The other options probe protected personal characteristics.

items.prompt: You have 120 applications for a role where a specific certification is a must-have. What should you do first when screening?

options.label: Shortlist applicants from well-known employers first, since their experience is easier to trust at screening
Rate each CV on how polished it looks, because presentation shows how carefully they would work
Read CVs until ten look strong, then stop reviewing the rest to save the team's limited time
Check every CV against the same must-have checklist and record the result before ranking anyone

rubric: Applying the same preset criteria to every application keeps screening consistent and fair.
Other options rely on stopping early, employer prestige or formatting, none of which are job criteria.

items.prompt: You are a candidate and the interviewer asks, 'What is your greatest weakness?' Which answer best applies good interview practice?

options.label: Name a real, minor weakness and describe the specific steps you are taking to improve it
List several serious weaknesses openly, because complete honesty always earns the most trust from interviewers
Say you work too hard, since presenting a strength as a flaw avoids giving anything negative away
Say you have no real weaknesses, because confidence shows you are ready for the role being offered

rubric: A real but manageable weakness plus concrete improvement shows self-awareness.
Disguised strengths, denial and oversharing each undermine credibility.

items.prompt: A panel has just finished interviewing a finalist. Which steps apply good debrief practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Where ratings on a criterion differ widely, interviewers cite their notes to explain the gap
Each interviewer submits scores independently before any discussion
Extra criteria are added after the interview to favour the candidate people liked most
The most senior interviewer speaks first to save time and set direction

rubric: Independent scores and evidence-based discussion of gaps keep the decision grounded.
Senior-first speaking anchors others; adding criteria afterward lets bias steer the outcome.

items.prompt: Two finalists have been scored on the same scorecard. Candidate A scores 3.8 overall with 4 out of 5 on SQL, a must-have. Candidate B scores 3.6 overall with 2 out of 5 on SQL, but the manager loved B's energy. What should the team do next?

options.label: Run a new round of different questions for B only, to give B another chance to reach the must-have
Offer to A, since A meets the must-have and has the higher score, and note B's energy as a separate point
Choose B, because energy cannot be scored and the manager's impression adds evidence the scorecard misses
Average the two candidates' scores with the manager's impression so that everyone's view counts equally

rubric: The decision should follow the criteria set in advance; A meets the must-have and scores higher.
Distractors let impressions override the scorecard or apply uneven processes to candidates.

items.prompt: You are building a structured interview for a customer support lead. A job analysis has produced five key competencies. Which step comes next?

options.label: Draft culture-fit questions so interviewers can judge who would get along best with the existing team
Prepare tailored questions from each résumé so every candidate can show their own particular strengths
Let interviewers hold informal chats first so they can form a view before they score anything formally
Write the same behavioral questions for each competency and define anchored rating scales for scoring

rubric: Structure comes from identical job-related questions with anchored scales built from the competencies.
Tailored or fit-based questions make candidates incomparable and let impressions drive scores.

items.prompt: You need a past-behavior question for the competency 'manages disagreement with stakeholders'. Which question fits that format?

options.label: Suppose a stakeholder pushed back hard on your project scope. What would you do first, and how would you handle it?
Would you say you are good at handling disagreement with stakeholders, and what makes you effective at it?
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a stakeholder over scope. What did you do?
What personal strength do you rely on most when working with difficult stakeholders, and why does it help?

rubric: A behavioral question asks for a specific past instance and its outcome.
The 'how would you' option is situational (hypothetical), and the others invite self-description.

items.prompt: A data analyst role has two must-haves: 3+ years of SQL and experience reporting to executives. A degree is not required. Which applicant should advance on these criteria?

options.label: 2 years of SQL, executive reporting, a master's degree in statistics
6 years of Python, strong referrals, employed at a well-known company
5 years of SQL, no reporting experience, a degree from a well-known university
3.5 years of SQL, monthly executive reporting, no degree

rubric: Only the second applicant meets both stated must-haves; the degree is not a criterion.
Other options rely on prestige, credentials or referrals rather than the stated criteria.

items.prompt: Your scorecard weights technical skill 50%, communication 30% and collaboration 20%. A candidate scores 4, 3 and 5 respectively out of 5. What is the weighted score?
rubric: 4.0 is the unweighted average; the others come from misapplied weights.

items.prompt: During an interview, a candidate mentions being pregnant while answering a question about availability. What should the interviewer do?

options.label: Acknowledge briefly, avoid follow-up questions on it, and score only on job-related criteria
Note the disclosure and lower the availability score slightly to reflect the risk of future leave
End the interview early so that nothing further is said that could create legal exposure
Ask about childcare plans to check the candidate can meet the schedule demands of the role

rubric: Protected information volunteered should not be probed or scored; evaluation stays on job-related criteria.
Other options use the information in the decision or penalise the candidate for disclosing.

items.prompt: You are drafting a job posting intended to attract a broad, qualified applicant pool. Which actions apply good practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Separate the must-have requirements from the nice-to-have ones
Replace phrases like 'rockstar ninja' with plain descriptions of the work
State the outcomes expected in the first year of the role
Raise the required experience to 10+ years to filter out weaker applicants
List every possible skill so no one is surprised later

rubric: Clear must-haves, plain language and defined outcomes make postings accurate and inclusive.
Inflated requirements and long wish lists deter qualified applicants without improving selection.

items.prompt: After a panel debrief, two interviewers gave the same candidate very different problem-solving scores: 4 and 2 on a 5-point anchored scale. Both used the same questions. The hiring manager wants to follow structured process. What should happen next?

options.label: Let the more senior interviewer's score prevail, since their experience makes their calibration more reliable than the other's
Have each interviewer cite notes evidence against the anchors, then rescore if warranted
Average the two scores to 3 and record it, so the debrief stays on schedule and neither interviewer is overruled
Ask a third interviewer who did not see the answers to give an overall impression as a tiebreaker rating

rubric: Structured process resolves gaps by comparing recorded evidence to anchors.
Averaging, seniority and gut-feel tiebreakers hide the disagreement or add noise.

items.prompt: A company finds that its interview scores barely predict new-hire performance. Interviews were unstructured conversations, and each interviewer gave one overall 'gut feel' score at the end. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Candidates prepared heavily with rehearsed answers, so responses showed polish rather than genuine ability
Questions and scoring varied, so scores reflected rapport and impressions more than job evidence
Interviewers were too lenient overall, so scores bunched at the top and a stricter scale would predict better
Too few interviewers took part, so each hire rested on limited opinions and adding more would fix it

rubric: Unstructured interviews with holistic ratings have low validity because impressions and rapport replace comparable evidence.
Leniency, preparation and headcount do not address the lack of consistent job-related criteria.

items.prompt: A panel process: interviewers meet after the last interview, the most senior person states a hire/no-hire view first, and then others submit written scores. Which step most undermines the independence of the evidence?

options.label: Holding a joint meeting after the interviews instead of having each interviewer send their evidence to the recruiter separately
Letting one person's hire/no-hire view be heard before the others have recorded their own ratings
Collecting written scores from interviewers instead of taking a verbal show of hands at the meeting
Waiting until every interview is finished before scores are recorded instead of scoring right after each one

rubric: Hearing a senior view before scoring anchors and conforms others' judgments.
Delayed scoring is a weaker flaw, though ideally scores are submitted promptly too.

items.prompt: You are hiring junior analysts, mostly career starters with little work history. Interviews use only behavioral 'tell me about a time at work' questions, and strong candidates are being rated low. What best explains this?

options.label: The panel is rating too harshly across the board, so the scale anchors should be moved down a point for these candidates
Junior candidates tend to communicate less clearly in interviews, which lowers their scores whatever the question format is
Career starters lack relevant work examples to draw on, so a work sample would show their skill more fairly
Behavioral questions are weak predictors of performance, so résumé review should replace them for entry-level roles

rubric: Behavioral questions depend on prior experience; for career starters a work sample or situational task elicits relevant evidence.
Other options overgeneralise or blame scale harshness rather than the mismatch between method and candidate pool.

items.prompt: Funnel data for one role. Application to screen pass: men 20%, women 19%. Screen to interview pass: men 50%, women 48%. Interview to offer: men 40%, women 15%. Where should you investigate first?

options.label: The sourcing channels, because the pass rates at the first stage are similar but not identical
The résumé screen, because small gaps early compound into large final differences
The offer stage only, because candidates may have withdrawn after the interview round
The interview-to-offer stage, because that is where outcomes diverge most sharply

rubric: The largest divergence occurs at interview-to-offer, pointing to the interview design, scoring or panel.
Early-stage gaps are small, and withdrawals would need separate data to support.

items.prompt: A hiring manager rejects a finalist with the note 'not a culture fit', citing no specific behavior or evidence. What is the main problem with this rationale?

options.label: It is too brief; adding a longer paragraph of the same impressions would make it acceptable
It should be replaced by a ranking of candidates by how much the team liked them
It is fine, because managers know their teams and are best placed to judge fit
It is a vague proxy that lets affinity bias in and cannot be checked against job-related criteria

rubric: Undefined 'fit' often masks similarity bias and cannot be audited against criteria.
Length, manager authority and likability rankings do not make the reasoning evidence-based.

items.prompt: You audit a hiring process. Which findings suggest that bias or noise is contaminating the evaluation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ratings are written after the group debrief discussion
Ratings use anchored descriptions tied to job competencies
Interviewers ask different questions of different candidates
Ratings correlate strongly with how long informal small talk lasted
Every interviewer records notes during the interview

rubric: Inconsistent questions, post-discussion ratings and rapport-correlated scores all weaken independent, job-related evidence.
Anchored scales and note-taking are good practice, not warning signs.

items.prompt: A firm lost five of six finalists to other employers. Timeline: screen within 3 days, interviews spread over 4 weeks because of panel scheduling, and offers sent 2 weeks after the last interview. Exit feedback said candidates 'accepted something sooner'. What is the most likely cause to address first?

options.label: The screening stage, because it let in candidates who were never serious about the job
The slow timeline, because strong candidates take faster competing offers
The offer salary, because candidates usually choose the highest-paying employer
The interview content, because finalists found the questions unrelated to the role

rubric: The long interview-to-offer timeline matches the feedback and is the clearest process cause.
Pay, screening and question content have no support in the stated evidence.

items.prompt: Four interviewers each interview the same finalists, but each picks their own questions and rates on a personal 1-10 scale. Scores for the same candidate range from 3 to 9. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Candidates varied their effort across rounds, because nervous people perform erratically with different strangers
Four interviewers is too many, because adding raters always increases disagreement in the final scores
Interviewers sampled different content and used different standards, so the ratings are not comparable
All four interviewers fell for a halo effect, because each overweighted the same early impression

rubric: Without common questions and anchored scales, raters measure different things, so scores diverge.
A shared halo effect would produce agreement, not spread; rater count is not the root cause.

items.prompt: Applicants for a role are 40% women. The resume-screen shortlist is 22% women. Later stages (interviews, offers) keep the shortlist's proportion. Where should the first investigation focus?

options.label: The interview rubric, because unstructured scoring tends to hide bias that appears at the end
The offer stage, because final decisions are where bias has the largest effect on outcomes
The sourcing channels, because the applicant pool must have been skewed before screening began
The screening criteria and how reviewers applied them, since the drop in representation occurs there

rubric: The proportion falls only at resume screening, so that stage's criteria and application need analysis first.
Other options point to stages where the data show no change.

items.prompt: A company hires only candidates scoring above 80 on a reasoning test. A year later, among those hires, test score barely correlates with performance ratings. A manager concludes the test is useless. What is the best analysis?

options.label: Range restriction: hires sit in a narrow score band, so the correlation is understated and says little about validity
Criterion contamination: managers who know the test scores rate their hires similarly, so the weak correlation reflects rater leniency
The manager is right: a weak correlation among current hires shows the test measures nothing related to job performance
Ceiling effect: the test is too easy for this group, so scores no longer separate strong from weak candidates among hires

rubric: Selecting only high scorers restricts the range and attenuates the observed correlation.
The manager's inference treats a restricted sample as if it represented all applicants.

items.prompt: A candidate describes leading a system migration but says 'we' throughout. Which follow-up best isolates the candidate's own contribution?

options.label: 'How large was the team, and what did the team accomplish overall by the end of the project?'
'What would you do differently if the migration ran again with the same team and timeline?'
'Walk me through one decision you personally made on that project and what happened next.'
'How did your teammates describe your leadership style in their feedback after the project?'

rubric: Asking for a specific personal decision and its result separates individual action from team outcomes.
The other probes stay at team level or invite opinion rather than evidence of individual behaviour.

items.prompt: Offer acceptance fell from 80% to 55%. Sourcing, screening and final-interview scores are unchanged. The median gap between final interview and offer grew from 3 to 12 days, and most decliners cite another offer. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Weaker candidates entered the funnel, because lower-quality sourcing normally reduces acceptance rates
Slow decisions after the final round let competing employers close candidates first
Interview scores were inflated, because candidates received offers they felt unprepared to accept
Pay was uncompetitive, because candidates always decline when the offer is below their expectations

rubric: The only changed variable is the delay, and decliners took other offers, pointing to speed.
Sourcing and score explanations contradict the stable data.

items.prompt: A debrief runs like this: the most senior interviewer states a verdict first, others speak in order of seniority, and two interviewers change their written scores during the meeting. Which problems does this show? Select all that apply.

options.label: Interviewers revising scores, which is always improper because new information must be ignored
Scores shifting after discussion, which hides what each interviewer actually observed
Speaking order by seniority, which lets status suppress dissenting views
Holding a discussion at all, because debriefs lower validity compared with simply averaging scores
Anchoring on the senior person's opinion before independent judgments are locked in

rubric: Senior-first verdicts, post-discussion score changes and status ordering all compromise independent evidence.
Revising scores is not always improper, and discussion itself is not the flaw.

items.prompt: A new analyst aced three technical interviews but struggles with stakeholders. The job analysis had listed stakeholder management as a top-three requirement. No interview stage asked about it. What is the most likely process gap?

options.label: Job-analysis criteria were not mapped to interview stages, so stakeholder skill went unmeasured
The technical interviews were too easy, so they selected people who lacked broader capabilities such as communication
Onboarding was too short, because skill gaps only emerge clearly after the first month on the job
The candidate hid weaknesses, because strong performers usually rehearse their answers for interviews

rubric: A requirement with no stage assessing it can't be evidenced; mapping criteria to stages closes the gap.
Other options blame difficulty, candidate deception or onboarding rather than the design flaw.

items.prompt: You must screen 500 applicants for a customer-support role. Criteria: strong predictive validity, under 60 minutes of candidate time, consistent scoring across graders, low cost per candidate. Which method fits best?

options.label: A single personality questionnaire used as the only pass or fail filter for every applicant
Two unstructured conversational interviews per applicant to gauge rapport and general impressions
A take-home case study of about six hours, graded by whichever manager happens to be free
A 45-minute simulated support-chat exercise scored with a standard rubric

rubric: A short job-simulation with a shared rubric meets validity, time, consistency and cost criteria.
The other options break the time limit, grader consistency or validity criteria.

items.prompt: The team fixed 'writes clear specifications' as a must-have, with a minimum score of 3/5, because it cannot be trained within a year. Candidate A scored 5/5 on four other criteria but 2/5 on this one. Candidate B scored 3/5 on all five. Which decision do the stated criteria best support?

options.label: Choose B, because A falls below the pre-set minimum on an untrainable must-have
Choose A, because a higher average score shows greater overall potential in the role
Reopen the search, because neither candidate is clearly strong on every criterion here
Choose A, because strengths on four criteria can offset the weak one within a year

rubric: The criteria were set in advance, and a failed untrainable must-have outweighs averages.
Choosing A relies on compensatory logic the stated criteria rule out.

items.prompt: Leaders propose scoring 'culture fit' by interviewer gut feel. Goals: protect team values and limit similarity bias. Which response is best?

options.label: Drop all values assessment, because any attempt to assess values brings unavoidable bias
Keep gut feel but add a second interviewer, because agreement between two reactions validates fit
Replace it with defined value-linked behaviours, each asked about and scored on anchored examples
Score fit only after the offer, because on-the-job results later show who truly fit the team

rubric: Defined behaviours with anchored scoring keep values assessment while reducing similarity bias.
Two gut reactions can share the same bias; dropping or postponing assessment fails the stated goals.

items.prompt: As a candidate for a product role, you're asked about your biggest weakness. A strong answer must be honest, not disqualifying for the role, and show action taken. Which answer best meets that?

options.label: 'I'm a perfectionist who works too hard, which sometimes frustrates people who care less about quality.'
'I over-built early prototypes; now I set a testing deadline first, and my last launch shipped two weeks sooner.'
'I struggle to prioritise customer needs, but I assume the company's training will fix that for me.'
'I have no major weaknesses in product work, though I'm always open to feedback from anyone.'

rubric: It names a real, non-fatal weakness and shows a concrete fix with a result.
Distractors are a disguised strength, a denial, or a disqualifying gap with no action by the candidate.

items.prompt: You're designing an interview loop for senior hires. Criteria: reliable ratings, every key competency assessed, under four hours of candidate time, offer within three weeks. Which design is best?

options.label: One expert interviewer covers every competency in a single long session, so scoring disagreement between raters cannot arise
Four trained interviewers each own different competencies, ask set questions and submit independent scores before the debrief
Eight interviewers each ask general questions and average their ratings, since extra raters raise reliability even with longer candidate time
Two rounds of open conversation with senior leaders, since unstructured talks give more time to reveal real competence

rubric: Four trained raters with distinct competencies and independent scoring meet reliability, coverage and time limits.
Eight repeated interviews break time limits; one rater is unreliable; open talks lack structure.

items.prompt: Judge which practices make an offer decision evidence-based, given the criteria: defensible, consistent, predictive. Select all that apply.

options.label: Weight a candidate's first five-minute impression above later evidence collected
Combine independent ratings against criteria fixed before interviewing began
Apply the same weighting rules to every finalist in the pool
Let the hiring manager override ratings when a candidate simply feels like a good fit
Record the reasons for the decision, tied explicitly to those criteria

rubric: Pre-set criteria, documented reasons and uniform weighting make decisions defensible and consistent.
Gut overrides and first-impression weighting reduce predictive value and consistency.

items.prompt: A director wants to skip the process and hire a friend's referral for an urgent role, with an offer within one week. Constraints: the decision must be defensible, fit quality matters, and the speed need is real. As recruiter, what is the best response?

options.label: Run a compressed structured loop: same job-related questions and rubric for the referral and two others in a day
Interview the referral with a full structured rubric now, and add other candidates later only if the referral scores poorly
Hire the referral on the director's endorsement, then use the structured interview afterward to plan onboarding and development
Hold to the normal four-week process for every candidate, since shortening a structured loop would weaken its predictive validity

rubric: A compressed structured loop meets the speed need while keeping decisions consistent and defensible.
Other options give up fairness, ignore the real urgency, or evaluate only one candidate.

items.prompt: A hiring lead says that because every panelist asks identical questions, calibrating how answers map to scores is unnecessary. Which critique is best?

options.label: Identical questions only help if panelists may also improvise follow-ups, because rigid scripts make candidates anxious, lower the validity of answers, and so make score calibration pointless.
Identical questions already remove rater bias, so calibration is worth doing only for legal paperwork and audit trails, and it does not change the quality of the scores.
Same questions standardise input, but raters still map answers to scores differently, so anchored rubrics and calibration are needed for reliability.
Calibration matters only for panels larger than five, because averaging across several raters already cancels out individual differences in how strictly each one scores.

rubric: Standardised questions do not standardise judgement; rater variance remains without anchors and calibration.
Distractors overstate what question standardisation achieves or treat calibration as optional or cosmetic.

items.prompt: You hire about four analysts a year. Criteria: strong prediction of job performance, low adverse impact, defensible to candidates. Which selection approach best meets all three?

options.label: A minimum years-of-experience filter followed by a consensus panel discussion, since experience reliably indicates performance.
A single cognitive ability test as the only gate, since it has high validity and is cheap to run for every applicant.
Unstructured conversations with senior leaders, since experienced judges can sense potential that formal tools miss entirely.
A rubric-scored job work sample combined with a structured behavioural interview, with both mapped to the same job analysis.

rubric: Work samples plus structured interviews combine good validity, lower adverse impact and clear job relevance.
A cognitive test alone carries adverse impact concerns; unstructured chats and experience filters have weaker validity.

items.prompt: Two finalists remain. A averages 4.3 across panelists, but one panelist scored A low, citing a concrete work-sample failure on a stated must-have. B averages 3.9 with no dissent. What is the best next step?

options.label: Examine the dissenter's evidence against the must-have criterion before combining scores, since specific evidence outweighs the mean.
Hire A, because the average is higher and one low score is most likely a harsh-rater effect that a panel mean is designed to absorb.
Drop the dissenting score as an outlier and recompute A's average, so that a single rater cannot swing a close decision between finalists.
Hire B, because consistency across panelists is a stronger predictor of success than a higher average that hides one panelist's disagreement.

rubric: Evidence-based dissent on a must-have should be tested against the criterion, not averaged away.
Distractors treat the mean or consistency as decisive, or discard the dissent as noise.

items.prompt: You must choose a debrief design that best limits anchoring and groupthink while still using every panelist's evidence. Which is best?

options.label: The hiring manager opens by sharing context and a preference, so panelists can interpret their notes against what the role truly needs.
Panelists submit written scores and evidence independently, then discuss only the criteria where scores diverge before any hiring decision.
Panelists discuss openly until everyone agrees, because forced consensus ensures the final decision is fully owned by the whole panel.
The most senior panelist votes last, so that their view can correct earlier scores and prevent the group from drifting off course.

rubric: Independent written scoring before discussion prevents early opinions from anchoring others.
Distractors let authority or consensus pressure shape judgements before evidence is recorded.

items.prompt: A candidate holds two offers. Criterion: find the best evidence of whether the hiring manager's stated priorities are real in practice. Which question to a recent hire gives the strongest evidence?

options.label: "What were your actual goals for the first 90 days, and how was your performance reviewed against them?"
"Does the manager seem supportive, and would you recommend the team to a friend looking for a role?"
"How does the company describe its values, and have you seen leaders refer to them in meetings?"
"How would you describe the team culture in three words, and does it match what the manager told me?"

rubric: Concrete goals and how they were reviewed reveal real priorities through behaviour, not through slogans.
Distractors ask for impressions, labels or stated values, which are easy to give without revealing actual priorities.

items.prompt: A team scores candidates on 'culture fit' by gut feel. Which critiques of this practice are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Fit scoring is safest when done last, after the debrief, so that it can break ties using the panel's overall feel.
Replacing fit with defined, behaviourally anchored value criteria keeps what is useful while making scores checkable.
Any consideration of values or working style is unlawful, so fit must be removed from all hiring criteria.
Undefined fit tends to reward similarity to existing staff, letting affinity bias pass as a job-related criterion.

rubric: Vague fit invites similarity bias; defined, anchored values criteria are a defensible fix.
Gut-feel tie-breaks add bias, and values-based criteria are not categorically unlawful.

items.prompt: A sales organisation finds that interview scores correlate only 0.1 with 12-month revenue among people it hired. Only candidates who scored above a high cut-off were hired, and the sample is 40 people. The VP concludes the interview is useless and proposes scrapping it. Which response is best justified?

options.label: Hold off, because range restriction and the small sample likely understate validity; check against broader criteria and wider data first.
Agree, but only if the correlation is recomputed after adding tenure and territory as controls, which would confirm the result.
Disagree, because any correlation from hired employees is unreliable, so the company should simply trust the original panel judgement.
Agree, because a correlation of 0.1 shows that the interview has almost no predictive value, and the cost of running it is not justified.

rubric: Only high scorers were hired, so range restriction shrinks the observed correlation, and n=40 is noisy.
Distractors accept a biased estimate, dismiss data entirely, or assume controls would confirm the conclusion.

items.prompt: You have 800 applicants for 5 roles and 10 recruiter hours. Constraints: names and schools hidden, screening must be job-relevant and consistently scored. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A review of applications in arrival order, stopping at 100, because early applicants show more motivation for the roles.
A short job-sample questionnaire with anonymised answers scored on a rubric, with the top band invited to structured interviews.
A keyword filter on CVs, with the top 50 by match count invited, because automation is consistent and quick to run.
A shortlist built from candidates at schools with the best past hire outcomes, since past success predicts future success.

rubric: Anonymised rubric-scored job samples are job-relevant, consistent and feasible in the hours given.
Keyword counts, arrival order and school pedigree are weakly job-relevant or bias-prone, or break the anonymity constraint.

items.prompt: The role needs a skill that almost no candidate has used before. Constraints: assess ability to learn, same process for everyone, and scorable by a rubric. Which interview component should you build?

options.label: Ask each candidate to describe a time they learned something quickly, and score how enthusiastic the story sounds to the panel.
Give a novel job-like task with a fixed hint sequence for everyone, and score how they use the hints and feedback against anchors.
Hire for the closest prior-experience match and plan to train after the offer, which avoids the need to assess learning in interviews.
Let each interviewer improvise a technical challenge in the new skill, which allows depth tailored to each candidate's background.

rubric: A standard novel task with fixed hints observes learning directly and is scorable with anchors.
Distractors rely on self-report, ignore the criterion, or break consistency across candidates.

items.prompt: A proposed process has competency-based questions, anchored rubrics and independent scoring. Which essential element is still missing?

options.label: A pre-agreed rule, set before meeting candidates, for combining scores and treating must-have criteria in the final decision.
A step where the panel reviews candidate social media profiles, so that culture signals missed in interviews can be added.
A policy allowing each panelist to add new questions when they sense a gap, so that the process adapts to each candidate.
A final gut-feel round with the hiring manager, so that intangible qualities not captured by the rubric can be weighed.

rubric: Without a prior decision rule, the panel can weight evidence after the fact to favour a preferred candidate.
Distractors reintroduce unstructured judgement or non-job-related information.

items.prompt: Top candidates keep declining because your process takes six weeks. Constraints: keep rigour, add no new bias, decide within two weeks. Which redesign fits?

options.label: Hold all structured steps in one scheduled loop with fixed scoring and a 48-hour decision deadline after the loop closes.
Drop the work sample and rely on one conversation with the hiring manager, which the manager can schedule within days.
Fast-track candidates who the recruiter feels are strongest, and give them a lighter process to speed up their offers.
Keep all steps in sequence but add an exploding offer deadline, so candidates feel urgency and decide before competitors do.

rubric: Batching structured steps and setting decision deadlines cuts time without losing rigour or consistency.
Distractors remove structure, apply unequal processes, or pressure candidates without shortening the process.

items.prompt: Rewrite a job ad to attract a diverse pool and still be accurate. Constraints: reflect real needs, avoid inflated requirements. Which approach is best?

options.label: Require ten years of experience to signal seniority, and welcome all applicants, which lets the best-qualified candidates stand out.
Describe year-one outcomes, list a few must-haves, and separate trainable nice-to-haves, so applicants can judge their fit accurately.
List every skill the team has ever wanted across past hires, so that candidates see the full ambition of the role and self-select appropriately.
Use vague, upbeat language about being a rockstar in a fast-paced team, so no group is put off by specific requirements.

rubric: Outcome-based, prioritised requirements are accurate and reduce self-exclusion from inflated lists.
Distractors inflate requirements or obscure the real role.

items.prompt: You must build an interview kit that is legally defensible, consistent across candidates and predictive of performance. Which elements must it include? Select all that apply.

options.label: The same core questions asked in the same order to every candidate.
Competencies derived from a documented job analysis of the role.
A single overall impression ranking that replaces criterion-level scores.
Anchored rubrics that define what weak, adequate and strong answers look like.
Interviewer-chosen resume deep-dives with no limits, to capture individual strengths.

rubric: Job analysis, anchored rubrics and common core questions give defensibility, consistency and validity.
Unlimited improvisation and holistic ranking undermine comparability and traceability.

items.prompt: A company will make 20 hires this year but has only three trained interviewers. Constraints: keep scoring independent and rubric-based, cut interviewer load, and still give candidates a good sense of the team. Which design best meets them?

options.label: Reduce to one interview with the hiring manager, who knows the role best and can judge fit and ability in a single conversation.
Have each trained interviewer own a competency using a shared kit, and use untrained staff only for unscored candidate-selling chats.
Have the three interviewers meet each candidate together in a panel, so that scores are discussed live and agreed on the spot.
Let any team member interview and score using their own questions, then average, since broad involvement spreads the workload.

rubric: Splitting competencies among trained raters keeps scores independent, while unscored chats let others help without adding noise.
Distractors lose consistency, independence or breadth of evidence.
